Check whether a hard-coded decomposer can stand in for the expensive human check in Amodei et al.'s setting.

in.other_title: Iterated Amplification: training signal built by combining solutions to easier subproblems
in.rationale: Amodei et al. ask how to ensure an agent respects aspects of an objective too expensive to evaluate often during training. Christiano et al. propose Iterated Amplification, which builds a training signal for problems too complicated for a human to evaluate by combining solutions to easier subproblems, and show it on 5 algorithmic tasks with a hard-coded decomposer; this is question answering, not an RL agent acting in an environment.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: how to train on objectives too expensive for a human to evaluate directly, via building a training signal from easier subproblems

open_obligations: Note that recursive reward modeling is a proposal without experiments in this record.

Check how exhaustive decomposition of evaluation is ensured, which Leike et al. flag as required.
in.other_title: Recursive reward modeling: agent A(k-1) assists the user in evaluating agent A(k)
in.rationale: Amodei et al. ask how an agent can respect objectives too expensive to evaluate frequently. Leike et al. propose recursive reward modeling, in which agent A(k-1) helps the user evaluate outcomes when training A(k), e.g. by summarising data or solving carved-off sub-problems; it is a proposal with no experiments.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: how to train RL agents on objectives users cannot cheaply evaluate, via reward modeling with agent assistance

text: Using a cleaning-robot example, the authors pose the question of how to efficiently ensure that the robot respects aspects of the objective too expensive to evaluate frequently during training, e.g. discarding candy wrappers but setting aside cellphones. Asking humans whether they lost anything can serve as a check but may have to be infrequent, so the robot must do the right thing despite limited information.
title: Scalable oversight question: respecting objectives too costly to evaluate during training
